# Removing All Seats Except Driver's + Front Passenger's One from Volkswagen Sharan 2nd gen. (2010)

Achieving a completely flat loading floor in a Volkswagen Sharan 2nd generation (produced from 2010) requires more than simply reclining the rear seatbacks. While folding the seats down provides a continuous surface from the front to the tailgate, it does not eliminate the bulk of the seat cushions, headrests, or the structural mounting points that protrude into the cargo volume. If your goal is to strip the vehicle down to only the driver and front passenger seats to maximize rear-deck utility, you are undertaking a significant interior modification.

The core technical challenge lies in the chassis structure and safety compliance of the 7-seater MPV platform. Unlike some modular commercial vans where seat rails can be completely stripped out, the Sharan's second generation integrates the rear seating into the floor pan with specific reinforcement beams. Removing these seats entirely involves disconnecting not just the upholstery, but also the load-bearing tracks bolted to the vehicle frame. You will need to locate and remove the bolts securing the seat rails to the floor tunnel. In many cases, these are high-tensile bolts designed to withstand crash forces; removing them requires a torque wrench or impact driver of sufficient capacity to avoid snapping fasteners in the aluminum or steel chassis members.

Once the mounting hardware is cleared, you must address the seat belts and tether points. The ISOFIX/LATCH anchors for child seats are bolted directly to the floor near the rear seat bases. Leaving these exposed creates a trip hazard and reduces usable cargo space. You will need to cut or unbolt the belt buckles and potentially drill out the mounting pins, though this permanently alters the vehicle's safety certification regarding rear seating integrity. If you plan to reseat the vehicle later, keep all hardware organized; if not, consider welding these points flush or capping them with filler material to prevent debris accumulation.

Another critical consideration is the center tunnel and transmission hump. The second-generation Sharan often features a pronounced transmission tunnel that runs beneath the rear seats. Even after removing the seating assemblies, this hump remains. To achieve a truly flat floor, you must inspect whether the tunnel height can be reduced without compromising the gear selector mechanism or shifter linkage. In some configurations, lowering the carpet and under-floor insulation around the transmission casing yields only a few millimeters of clearance, but it might not eliminate the step entirely unless the entire rear floor pan is modifiedâa task requiring professional welding skills to ensure structural rigidity.

From a safety perspective, removing rear seats fundamentally changes the vehicle's crash dynamics. The original design relies on specific crumple zones and occupant protection structures that assume full seating capacity. Without rear passengers, the center of gravity shifts, potentially affecting handling characteristics during emergency maneuvers. Furthermore, insurance policies may void coverage if the vehicle is modified in a way that violates local regulations regarding seat belt availability or structural integrity. Ensure you check with your insurer before proceeding, as some jurisdictions require specific seat configurations for road legality.

If your primary use case involves transporting large equipment where every cubic centimeter matters, this modification is feasible but labor-intensive. You will need to remove the plastic trim panels covering the footwells, disconnect the airbag connectors (if present on the rear outboard seats), and carefully extract the seat mechanisms without damaging the floor anchors. The process essentially turns the Sharan into a 2-seater with a bulk cargo hold, but it comes at the cost of structural complexity and regulatory compliance.
